data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Decentralized networks are more resilient to correlated failure provided they maintain 'stack diversity', whereas large services suffer from 'redundancy paradoxes' where internal duplication scales the impact of a single systemic bug.","counterconditions":[{"case":"Economic pressures lead small operators to converge on a single 'best-of-breed' cloud provider or framework (Economic Homogeneity).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The decentralized network relies on a single shared discovery mechanism (e.g., a global DNS root) that becomes the primary correlated failure point.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The 'Redundancy Paradox' posits that strictly increasing internal redundancy in a monolith (e.g., more identical nodes) increases the probability that a single latent bug in the coordination logic or shared codebase will trigger a simultaneous, global crash. Conversely, a decentralized network distributes failure risk across heterogeneous implementations, ensuring that a bug in one service's stack does not propagate to others unless they share a deep-substrate dependency.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
